title: Clocks, trains and rates
objectives: Solve clock-angle and meeting problems in one line of algebra.

screens.title: Two hands, two speeds
screens.prose: Slide the clock on from 12:00. The caption gives each hand's position in degrees, clockwise from 12. Watch how fast each one turns.

derive.caption: {{floor(m / 60) < 1 ? 12 : floor(m / 60)}}:{{m - 60 * floor(m / 60) < 10 ? "0" : ""}}{{round(m - 60 * floor(m / 60), 0)}}. Minute hand at {{round(6 * (m - 60 * floor(m / 60)), 1)}}°, hour hand at {{round(0.5 * m, 1)}}°, both clockwise from 12.

screens.question: What is the angle between the hands at 3:40, in degrees?

hints.text: 3:40 is 220 minutes past 12:00. Slide there.
The minute hand is at 240° and the hour hand at 110°.

feedback.correct: 130°. The hour hand has moved 20° past the 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read both hands at 220 minutes and subtract.

byKey.stuck: You left the hour hand on the 3. In 40 minutes it moves on 20°, to 110°.
byKey.reflex: That is the angle the long way round. The angle between the hands is the smaller one, 130°.

explain.text: At 3:40 the minute hand is at 240° and the hour hand at 110°. The hour hand turns half a degree a minute, so it is 20° past the 3. The gap is 130°.

screens.title: When the hands meet
screens.prose: At 3:00 the minute hand is 90° behind the hour hand. Each minute it turns 6° and the hour hand turns 0.5°.

derive.caption: {{floor(m / 60) < 1 ? 12 : floor(m / 60)}}:{{m - 60 * floor(m / 60) < 10 ? "0" : ""}}{{round(m - 60 * floor(m / 60), 0)}}. Minute hand at {{round(6 * (m - 60 * floor(m / 60)), 1)}}°, hour hand at {{round(0.5 * m, 1)}}°, both clockwise from 12.

screens.question: How many minutes after 3:00 do the hands first meet? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: How fast does the 90° gap close?
The minute hand gains 6 − 0.5 = 5.5° a minute.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the gap by the rate at which it closes.

byKey.still: You divided by 6, as if the hour hand stood still. It moves 0.5° a minute too.
byKey.added: You added the speeds. Both hands turn the same way, so the gap closes at the difference.

explain.text: The gap of 90° closes at 5.5° a minute, so it closes in $90/5.5 = 16\tfrac{4}{11}$ minutes, about 3:16:22. The hands meet every $720/11 = 65\tfrac{5}{11}$ minutes, 11 times in 12 hours. Principle: two movers close at the difference of their speeds.

screens.title: A car chases a lorry
screens.prose: A lorry at 72 km/h is 6 km ahead of a car at 90 km/h. Both drive the same way. Slide time on and watch the gap.

derive.caption: After {{round(t, 0)}} minutes: car at {{fixed(1.5 * t, 1)}} km, lorry at {{fixed(6 + 1.2 * t, 1)}} km.

screens.question: How many minutes does the car take to draw level?

hints.text: By how much does the gap shrink each hour?
The car gains 90 − 72 = 18 km each hour.
6 km at 18 km/h takes a third of an hour.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find how fast the 6 km gap closes.

byKey.ignore: You let the lorry stand still: 6 km at 90 km/h. The lorry moves on as well.
byKey.sum: You added the speeds. That is for cars driving towards each other.

explain.text: The gap of 6 km closes at 90 − 72 = 18 km/h. So it closes in 6/18 of an hour, which is 20 minutes. Principle: ride with the slower mover and only the difference of speeds matters.

screens.title: There and back
screens.prose: You drive 120 km to a client at 60 km/h. You drive the same road back at 40 km/h.
screens.question: What is your average speed for the round trip, in km/h?

options.why: You averaged the two speeds. The slow leg takes longer, so it weighs more.
You added the speeds. An average speed lies between the two.

hints.text: Find the time of each leg first.
Out takes 2 hours and back takes 3 hours.
240 km in 5 hours.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the whole distance by the whole time.

byKey.a: 50 is the average of the speeds. You spend 3 hours at 40 and only 2 at 60, so the average is lower.
byKey.s: You added the speeds. The average must lie between 40 and 60.

explain.text: Out takes 2 hours and back takes 3, so 240 km take 5 hours: 48 km/h. The slow leg lasts longer, so it pulls the average below 50. Principle: over equal distances, add the times, not the speeds.

screens.title: A target average
screens.prose: You drive 20 km out at 40 km/h. You want to average 80 km/h over the 40 km round trip.
screens.question: How fast must you drive back?

options.why: You set the plain average of 40 and the return speed to 80. Equal distances do not average that way.
At 160 km/h the trip back takes 7.5 minutes. The 40 km then take 37.5 minutes, an average of 64 km/h.

hints.text: How long may 40 km take at an average of 80 km/h?
It may take 30 minutes. The trip out took 30 minutes.
No time is left for the trip back.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn the average into a time budget.

byKey.120: 120 is what the plain average needs. Time 40 km at 80 km/h: 30 minutes, all used on the way out.
byKey.160: At 160 km/h the round trip takes 37.5 minutes, so the average is 64 km/h.

explain.text: Averaging 80 km/h over 40 km allows 30 minutes in all. The trip out already took those 30 minutes. Principle: turn an average speed into a time budget before you choose a speed.

screens.title: Rates in one line
screens.prose: Each answer came from a rate times a time. At $h$:$m$ the hands are $$\theta = |30h - 5.5m|$$ degrees apart; take $360 - \theta$ if $\theta > 180$. Two movers close at the **relative speed**. Equal distances average to the **harmonic mean**, $\tfrac{2ab}{a + b}$. Zhou's green book (its brainteasers chapter), Crack's *Heard on the Street* and Joshi and co-authors all set such openers.
screens.question: At 12:00, with $h = 12$ and $m = 0$, what is the angle between the hands?

hints.text: Work out $|30 \cdot 12 - 0|$ first.
It is 360, which is more than 180.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the rule for an angle above 180.

byKey.raw: The formula gives 360, which is more than 180. Take 360 − 360 = 0.

explain.text: The formula gives $|360 - 0| = 360$, a whole turn. Above 180 we take $360 - \theta$, which is 0. Principle: check a formula at the edge of its range.

screens.title: Why the harmonic mean
screens.prose: Drive a distance $d$ out at speed $a$ and back at speed $b$. Order the lines that give the average speed. Two lines may swap, and one does not belong.
screens.question: Order the derivation.

lines.text: Average speed is distance over time: $\dfrac{2d}{d/a + d/b}$.
Multiply top and bottom by $ab$: $\dfrac{2ab}{a + b}$.
Each leg is half the trip, so the average is $\tfrac{a + b}{2}$.
lines.why: Each leg is half the distance, not half the time. The slow leg takes longer.

hints.text: Average speed is total distance over total time.
Write both totals before dividing.
Then clear the small fractions: divide by $d$, multiply by $ab$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the totals before you divide.

byKey.d1: The legs are equal in distance, not in time, so the plain average is wrong.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the plain average belongs.

explain.text: Total distance $2d$ over total time $d/a + d/b$ gives $\tfrac{2ab}{a + b}$ once $d$ cancels. With 60 and 40 it gives $4800/100 = 48$. Principle: an average speed is always total distance over total time.

screens.title: Drill: quarter past nine
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. The clock reads 9:15.
screens.question: What is the angle between the hands, in degrees?

hints.text: Use $|30h - 5.5m|$ with $h = 9$ and $m = 15$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find both hands, then take the smaller angle.

byKey.raw: 187.5 is the angle the long way round. Take 360 − 187.5 = 172.5.
byKey.stuck: You left the hour hand on the 9. By 9:15 it has moved 7.5° towards the 10.

explain.text: The minute hand is at 90° and the hour hand at 277.5°. They are 187.5° apart one way and 172.5° the other. Principle: the hour hand is never exactly on its number except on the hour.

screens.title: Drill: twenty past two
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. The clock reads 2:20.
screens.question: What is the angle between the hands, in degrees?

hints.text: Place the hour hand first.
The hour hand is at $60 + 10 = 70°$ and the minute hand at 120°.
Subtract.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the hour hand on for the 20 minutes.

byKey.stuck: You left the hour hand on the 2. In 20 minutes it moves 10° on.
byKey.reflex: That is the long way round. Take the smaller angle.

explain.text: The minute hand is at 120° and the hour hand at 70°. So the hands are 50° apart. Principle: $|30h - 5.5m| = |60 - 110| = 50$ agrees.

screens.title: Drill: right angles
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Count from 12:00 up to, but not including, the next 12:00.
screens.question: How many times in those 12 hours are the hands at right angles?

hints.text: The minute hand gains 5.5° a minute. How much does it gain in 12 hours?
It gains $5.5 \cdot 720 = 3960°$, which is 11 laps.
Each lap passes 90° and 270° once.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the laps the minute hand gains on the hour hand.

byKey.hourly: Twice an hour gives 24, but the minute hand gains only 11 laps in 12 hours.
byKey.once: Each lap holds two right angles: at 90° ahead and at 90° behind.
byKey.day: 44 is for a whole day. The question asks for 12 hours.

explain.text: In 12 hours the minute hand gains 11 laps on the hour hand. Each lap passes a right angle twice, so 22 times. Principle: count events by the laps of the relative motion.

screens.title: Drill: two pipes
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. One pipe fills a tank in 4 hours and another in 12 hours.
screens.question: How many hours do both pipes take together?

hints.text: Add the rates, not the times.
The pipes fill $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and $\tfrac{1}{12}$ of the tank an hour.
$\tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{12} = \tfrac{1}{3}$ of the tank an hour.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add what each pipe fills in one hour.

byKey.mean: You averaged the times. Two pipes together are faster than either alone.
byKey.sum: You added the times. That is one pipe after the other, not both at once.

explain.text: Together the pipes fill $\tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{12} = \tfrac{1}{3}$ of the tank an hour. So the tank takes 3 hours. Principle: rates add; times do not.

screens.title: Opposite hands in a day
screens.prose: Follow-up. The interviewer now asks about a whole day, from 00:00 up to 24:00. The hands are opposite at 6:00, for instance. A desk counts recurring events the same way, by laps of the relative motion.
screens.question: How many times in the day do the hands point in opposite directions?

hints.text: Use the laps the minute hand gains, as for right angles.
In 12 hours it gains 11 laps, and each lap passes 180° once.
A day holds two lots of 12 hours.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the gained laps over 24 hours.

byKey.half: 11 is the count for 12 hours. The day has 24.
byKey.hourly: Once an hour gives 24, but the minute hand gains only 22 laps in a day.
byKey.right: 44 counts right angles in a day. Opposite means 180°, once a lap.

explain.text: In 24 hours the minute hand gains 22 laps on the hour hand. Each lap passes 180° exactly once, so 22 times. Principle: count events by the laps of the relative motion.

ideas: Write each position as a rate times a time: the hands turn 6° and 0.5° a minute.
Two movers close at the difference of their speeds, or the sum when they approach.
Over equal distances the average speed is the harmonic mean, below the plain mean.

formula.name: Clock angle
formula.note: The hands meet every 720/11 minutes, 11 times in 12 hours.

summary.trap: Out at 60 km/h and back at 40 averages 48, not 50: the slow leg takes longer.

quiz.prose: You buy £100 of a stock at £40 a share, then £100 more at £60 a share.
quiz.question: What average price per share have you paid, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the pounds spent by the shares bought.

byKey.mean: £50 averages the prices. You bought more shares at £40, so the average is lower.

explain.text: £100 buys 2.5 shares at £40 and 1.67 at £60. So £200 buys 4.17 shares, £48 each. Principle: equal amounts at two prices average to the harmonic mean.

quiz.prose: A moving walkway is 60 m long and runs at 1 m/s. You walk along it, the same way, at 1.5 m/s.
quiz.question: How many seconds does the walkway take you?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add your speed to the walkway's speed.

byKey.diff: You subtracted the speeds. You walk with the walkway, so the speeds add.
byKey.walk: 40 s is your walk on the ground. The walkway carries you too.

explain.text: On the walkway you move at 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 m/s. So 60 m take 60/2.5 = 24 seconds. Principle: speeds in the same frame add.

quiz.question: What is the angle between the hands, in degrees?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The hour hand is halfway from 6 to 7.

byKey.stuck: You put both hands on the 6. By 6:30 the hour hand has moved 15° on.
byKey.reflex: That is the long way round. Take the smaller angle.

explain.text: The minute hand is at 180° and the hour hand at 195°. So the hands are 15° apart. Principle: $|30 \cdot 6 - 5.5 \cdot 30| = |180 - 165| = 15$.

quiz.prose: A tap fills a tank in 6 hours. A drain empties the full tank in 9 hours. Both are open on an empty tank.
quiz.question: How many hours does the tank take to fill?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the drain's rate from the tap's rate.

byKey.diff: You subtracted the times. Subtract the rates instead.
byKey.sum: You added the times. The drain works against the tap, so subtract rates.

explain.text: Each hour the tank gains $\tfrac{1}{6} - \tfrac{1}{9} = \tfrac{1}{18}$. So it fills in 18 hours. Principle: rates add with a sign; times never do.
